place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 药园 · 又三年
place.en: Chending Temple · The herb garden · Three more years

setup.zh: 年六那年秋天，秦雁把执事堂西墙上一块新牌往你手里一递：下邳北道，吃人的熊，三条命。
setup.en: In the autumn of the sixth year Qin Yan hands you a new tag from the Hall of Errands' wall: the north road out of Xiapi, a man-eating bear, three lives.

recap.zh: 年六，下邳道上吃人的老熊，剑从它吼那一霎的缝里进去，八层；「飘风不终朝」，「进退，利武人之贞」，九层；丹房后头一口自己的炉子，第五炉出一颗一纹的——「我炼的」；第五年腊八你随风、入隙，差一霎赢了大比，观里那颗一转的官丹，揭了封，米汤粘回去，收进了储物袋——转天闵丹师在丹房门口跟你打了个照面，鼻子动了一动；入秋，九层圆满。
recap.en: Year six: the man-eating old bear on the Xiapi road, the sword in through the seam the instant it roared, layer eight; 'a gale does not last a morning', 'it profits a warrior to hold firm', layer nine; a furnace of your own behind the pill house, one one-ring pill in the fifth batch — "I made it"; at Laba in the fifth year you won the contest by an instant, going with the wind and entering the gap; the temple's one-turn pill, its seal lifted and glued back with rice water, went into the storage pouch — next day Pill-master Min met you at the pill-house door, and his nose twitched; by autumn, layer nine, Consummation.

zh: 「姑娘，五年前你押过他一回。」「输了。」
en: "Miss, five years ago you bet on him once." "Lost."

story.zh:
年六，沈小满十七岁，练气七层，在这一层上卡住了。卡他的是一道缝：师父瞿老教他巽四的剑，教到入隙，石头的缝他看得见了，活东西身上的缝，他看不见。白天他揭执事堂的差事牌，替丹房的闵丹师看炉、碾药；腰里一口暗红的铜剑，叫火柴，脚上一双鯥皮鞋，叫顺风溜——背着风退一步，一滑十丈，逆着风，屁用没有。

那年秋天，沉鼎观执事堂西墙上挂出一块新牌：下邳北道，吃人的熊，三条命。揭牌的是秦雁——第二年进的内门，这时候八层。她在墙底下站了很久，揭下来，回过头，正撞上小满的眼睛。她什么也没说，把牌子往他手里一递。她爹是猎户，叫熊咬了腿，躺了八年。

下邳北道是一条山路，两边是崖。三条命，都是走夜路的脚夫，都是在同一个拐弯上没的。秦雁蹲在拐弯上看了半天，道：「上头。」崖半腰一个石洞，洞口的草全往里倒。小满看了看地上的爪印，一个巴掌把他的手整个盖进去还有余，道：「老熊。皮厚。」阿禾道：「箭进不去？」小满道：「进得去，不够深。」

阿禾的法子是烟。孙二狗砍了半天湿柴，背上来堆在洞口，点着了，拿一块松木板扇。烟进了洞，洞里便起了一声吼，像山裂了一道缝。那熊出来的时候，四个人都没想到它有那么大：人立起来，比洞口还高，一身的黑毛全立着，眼睛给烟熏得通红。它看见的头一个，是扇风的孙二狗。

孙二狗没跑。他把那块松木板竖起来，挡在胸口。一掌下来，木板碎成四片，孙二狗飞出去一丈远，撞在崖壁上，滑下来，坐在地上。众人只当他完了，他却扶着崖壁站了起来，一条胳膊耷拉着，另一条胳膊把一片碎木板又举起来，嘴里说：「沈、沈师兄——」

那熊第二掌没落下去。秦雁的剑到了。那是一口下阶法器，剑气出鞘三尺，直奔它的眼睛。老熊一偏头，剑气在它额上犁出一道血槽，它便撇下孙二狗，转过来，再一次人立起来，冲着秦雁。

人立起来的熊，胸口是空的。小满的爹说过，鹿最好射的是落脚的那一下；熊，是立起来的那一下。这一下他等了半天。弓是满的，离着两丈，一箭进了胸口——进了三寸，没了。它皮上裹着那层东西，他在崖顶上看了大半年石头的缝，这时候看见了：那层光跟着它的灵力走，它一吼，一身的灵力全涌到那一声吼上，胸口那层光便薄了一霎。缝在这里。

第二声吼起来的时候，小满已经在它胸口底下了。火柴出鞘，七层的火柴灌满了灵力，剑刃发烫，烫得握剑的手心冒汗；他没砍，是送——顺着那薄了一霎的地方，剑进去了，没有一点声息，像风钻进了门缝，一直进到剑柄。老熊低下头，看了看胸口那只握剑的手，往前走了两步，倒在了秦雁脚边。秦雁的剑还举着，剑尖上一滴血，挂了很久很久，才落下去。

小满拔出剑来，手还在抖。

熊胆是秦雁割的。她把那颗胆拿油纸包了，揣进怀里，一句话也没说。孙二狗那条胳膊断了两处。阿禾当夜把他按在火堆边上，念了一句《阴符经》头一篇的头一句，两只手按在断处，拿自己的生气往里送——两头的骨茬像两垄芽，互相够着、缠上，血先止了；她的脸一点一点白下去，指尖那一点青一点一点淡下去。送到「死不了」，她停了手，小满给他吞了一颗一道纹的回春丹。天亮接上了，疼了半个月。县里谢了五两银子，牌子翻过来，灵石三块。秦雁把那三块灵石分给他们三个，一人一块，自己一块没留。小满道：「师姐揭的牌。」秦雁道：「挨打的是他。」又看了小满一眼，「杀的是你。」她那只总按着袖口的左手，这一回没有按。
story.en:
Year six. Shen Xiaoman was seventeen, layer seven of Qi Refining, and stuck there. What held him was a seam: his master Old Qu had taught him the sword of Xun the fourth as far as Entering-the-gap, and the seams in stone he could see now; the seams in a living thing he could not. By day he took tags from the Hall of Errands; by night he kept the furnace and ground herbs for Pill-master Min of the pill house. At his waist hung a dark-red copper sword called the Matchstick; on his feet, a pair of Lu-hide shoes called the Tailwind Slide — step back with the wind behind you and you slide ten zhang; against the wind they're no damn use at all.

That autumn a new tag went up on the wall of the Hall of Errands at Chending Temple: the north road out of Xiapi, a man-eating bear, three lives. The one who took it down was Qin Yan — in the inner court since the second year, layer eight by now. She stood under the wall a long while, took it down, turned, and met Xiaoman's eyes. She said nothing, and put the tag into his hand. Her father was a hunter; a bear had taken him by the leg, and he had been eight years abed.

The north road out of Xiapi was a mountain road with cliffs on both sides. The three lives were all porters walking it by night, all lost at the same bend. Qin Yan squatted at the bend a long while and said: "Above." Halfway up the cliff was a cave, the grass at its mouth all bent inward. Xiaoman looked at the prints on the ground — one paw would have covered his whole hand with room to spare. "An old bear. Thick hide." "Arrows won't go in?" said A-He. "They'll go in," said Xiaoman. "Not deep enough."

A-He's plan was smoke. Sun Ergou spent half a day cutting green wood, carried it up and heaped it at the cave mouth, lit it, and fanned it with a pine board. The smoke went into the cave, and out of the cave came a roar like the mountain splitting. When the bear came out, none of the four had reckoned on anything so big: standing up, it was taller than the cave mouth, every black hair on end, its eyes red from the smoke. The first thing it saw was Sun Ergou with his board.

Sun Ergou did not run. He stood the pine board up in front of his chest. One blow, and the board was in four pieces; Sun Ergou flew ten feet, hit the cliff wall, slid down and sat. The others gave him up for done — but he got to his feet against the cliff, one arm hanging, and with the other he raised a shard of board again, saying: "Sh-shen-shixiong —"

The second blow never fell. Qin Yan's sword arrived — a low-grade artifact whose edge-qi ran three feet out of the sheath, straight for the eyes. The old bear turned its head; the qi ploughed a bloody furrow across its brow, and it left Sun Ergou, swung round, and stood up a second time, facing Qin Yan.

A bear standing up has nothing over its chest. Xiaoman's father used to say a deer is easiest shot as it lands a foot; a bear, as it rears. He had waited half the night for this. The bow was full, two zhang off; an arrow into the chest — three inches, and no further. The hide was wrapped in that layer; he had spent most of a year on the clifftop looking at seams in stone, and now he saw it: the light moved with the bear's qi, and when it roared, all of it rushed into the roar, and for an instant the light over the chest thinned. There was the seam.

As the second roar rose, Xiaoman was already under its chest. The Matchstick came out, a layer-seven Matchstick full of qi, the edge running hot, hot enough to sweat the hand that held it; he did not cut — he sent it, along that thinned place, and the sword went in without a sound, like wind through a door-crack, all the way to the hilt. The old bear lowered its head and looked at the hand holding the sword in its chest, walked two steps forward, and fell at Qin Yan's feet. Qin Yan's sword was still raised, a drop of blood on its point that hung a long, long time before it fell.

Xiaoman drew the sword out, his hand still shaking.

It was Qin Yan who cut out the gall. She wrapped it in oilpaper and tucked it into her jacket without a word. Sun Ergou's arm was broken in two places. That night A-He sat him by the fire, recited the first line of the first chapter of the *Yinfu Jing*, laid both hands on the break and sent her own living qi into it — the two ends of bone reached for each other like two rows of sprouts and knit, and the bleeding stopped first; her face went whiter by degrees, the trace of green at her fingertips fainter by degrees. When it reached 'won't die of it' she took her hands away, and Xiaoman gave him a one-ring mending pill. By dawn it was set; it hurt for half a month. The county sent five taels in thanks; the tag was turned, three spirit stones. Qin Yan gave the three stones to the three of them, one each, and kept none. "Sister, you took the tag," said Xiaoman. "He took the beating," said Qin Yan. She looked at Xiaoman again. "You did the killing." The left hand that was always pressed to her sleeve was not pressed there this time.

label.en: Laba · Up on the stage again

exits.means: year six the man-eating 老熊 with 秦雁 — the arrow stops at three inches, the sword goes in through the seam as it roars (入隙 lands); 孙二狗's arm healed by 阿禾's 生 and a one-ring pill; 八层; year seven 飘风不终朝 (定风 = waiting it out), 进退 (「初六：进退，利武人之贞」; the pine bough), 九层, the 火柴's line of sparks; a furnace of his own, a true 一纹 pill, 「我炼的」; at Laba in year five he goes up again after four years away, Shopkeeper Qian lists him at one-pays-fifty, A-He's single cash is the only stake; the final against a 九层圆满 won by an instant with 随风 and 入隙, a cut under the ribs; Qian counts out fifty-one cash to her; the sect's one-turn pill resealed with rice water into the storage pouch; 闵丹师's sniff after five years at one furnace; five brides on the Zhang

story.zh:
那年冬天，他过了八层。

每年十月十八，周衡一整天不翻账簿，巡夜的蜡烛也不掰了；每年除夕他去一趟正殿，出来都是那一句「明年，弟子再来」。小满不问。秦雁第五年筑了基，调去了别处的差事；孙二狗两年一层，一层到三层，爬上一层便在大通铺门口哭一回；阿禾那一小条地年年种，年年多半是瘪穗。瞿老只给他定过一条规矩：「差事，去得。蒙山的牌子，不许揭——镜子那头的人，知道你是哪里来的。」家信一年两封，他娘的字仍旧又小又密：屋顶不漏了；你爹的膝盖，阴天疼，晴天也疼。内门的单间一间也没空出来，他仍旧睡在西廊那间屋最靠门的那张铺上。大比年年比，头几年，他不上台——他还不到九层，拿了那颗筑基丹也只能揣着，倒招一观的眼睛。

瞿老那年夏天教的，说是一式，其实是一句话。小满问他：「师父，熊那一声吼，为什么一定会来？」瞿老道：「因为它停不住。」他念了一句书：「《道德经》{典=laozi-piaofeng}里说：『飘风不终朝，骤雨不终日。』大风刮不了一早上，暴雨下不了一整天。天地都撑不久的事，它撑得了？」他点起一根蜡烛，搁在青石上：「你吹吹看。」小满鼓起腮帮子，使劲吹，火苗子贴着蜡烛倒下去，倒成一条线，可就是不灭；他吹到没气了，火苗子直起来，还是那样。瞿老道：「你吹不灭它。你吹到没气了，它还在。定风，不是站着不动。是等它吹完。」

他这才明白，田埂上的七口，河滩上的三回，熊那一声吼，是一回事。

八层到九层，瞿老教的是进退。那是秋天，他把扫帚把在地上一点，道：「《周易》{典=zhouyi-xun}里，巽卦头一爻，开口两个字：『进退。』整句是：『初六：进退，利武人之贞。』」他拿扫帚把在青石上写了那六个字，「进进退退，是心里拿不定；拿得定的，是武人——一剑出去，全部的灵力，没有退的那一半。」他指着崖边一根碗口粗的松枝：「你砍它。」

小满砍了。一剑下去，剑卡在松枝里，拔不出来——他压进去的是大半口气，留了小半口，怕砍空了收不回来。瞿老道：「你给自己留了一口。」小满拔出剑，又砍，这一回他把丹田里的灵力整个压进剑里，什么也没留，松枝「咔嚓」一声落了地，剑过去，人也过去，收不住，往前冲了两步才站住，缸里一滴灵力也没有了，腿软得像面条。瞿老道：「这才是进退。」他看着崖下，又添了一句，声音低得几乎听不见：「巽四这一宫的剑，不怕慢，不怕软，就怕进退。进了一半想退，那一剑，自己先散了。」顿了一顿，「……剑是这样，别的，也是这样。」

小满那时候没听懂这一句添的是什么。那年腊月之前，他九层了，吸和吐之间，听不出缝来。九层的火柴，一剑出去，剑尖上会甩出一线火星子，细得像灶膛里崩出来的那种——他不知道那是什么，瞿老也没说。

那年秋天，他在丹房后头那间小屋里，有了一口自己的炉子。是闵丹师炼废了不要的，炉壁裂了一道缝，拿泥糊上了；炉底接着丹房那眼地火分出来的一道细缝，火小得像灯芯，一炉只炼三颗。闵丹师只说了一句：「料你自己碾，火你自己看。炼糊了，碾了做药引。」头一炉，三颗全糊了。第二炉，两颗糊了，一颗没转起来，是一团黑。第五炉，出了一颗，青白，一道纹，歪歪扭扭的，像孩子写的字。他捧着那颗丹去给闵丹师看，闵丹师捏起来，转了一圈，闻了闻，道：「有火气。」又道：「能吃。」这是五年里他从闵丹师嘴里听见的最长的一句夸奖。打这以后，有人问起他手里的丹，他便说：「我炼的。」这一句是真的；饭桶吐的那些一道纹两道纹的，混在他自己炼的那些一道纹里头，谁也分不出来——只有一样分得出：他炼的有火气，饭桶的没有。他拿一颗饭桶的，对着自己那口炉子看了半天，想：要是把它放进去，过一回火呢？他没放。他把那颗丹收回了怀里。

那一年腊月，钱掌柜照旧把板子扛上了山，在老槐树底下支开摊子。板上头几行，仍旧是内门的；最底下一行，写的是：**沈小满　一赔五十。**

有人问：「九层了，还一赔五十？」钱掌柜拨着算盘道：「杂灵根拿头名，三百年没出过。」又拨了一下，「四年没上过台。全观记得的沈小满，是四层的、浑身是血、挂在树上的那一个——九层的他出手，谁见过？没见过的，我往大里写。」

阿禾挤到秤盘跟前，放下一文钱。钱掌柜抬起眼皮：「姑娘，五年前你押过他一回。」阿禾道：「输了。」钱掌柜道：「还押？」阿禾道：「他四年没上台，我没处押。」接了纸条，揣好，走了。那一年押沈小满的，统共一文钱。

第五年腊八，刮的是北风。头一场，小满抽着的是内门一个火行的九层。他上了台，头一件事不是看人，是看演武场边上那面旗——旗往南扯。先看风，后看鹿；身后没人替他说，他自己说。他往北边那块青石板上一站，便不挪了。那师兄的火弹一颗接一颗打过来，他拿土墙接，接一颗，碎一面，满台是烟；烟顺着北风，全往南倒，倒进那师兄自己的眼睛里。那师兄咳一声，退半步，咳得眼泪鼻涕一大把，咳到第七声，退到了台边。小满这才走过去，伸手推了一把。掉下台的，输。

中间三场，一场靠脚，一场靠数，一场靠对面那人自己急了，没一场打得好看。决赛的对手，是内门一个九层圆满，等那颗丹等了九年，一上台便是全力，金刃一道接一道。小满躲得开的躲，躲不开的随——随风，剑贴着那金刃往旁边一引，刃上的劲卸去一半，剩下的一半照旧把他往后犁出半尺，脚底下那块厚地稳着；引不开的那几道，挨。半炷香烧到一半，他左边肋下已经开了一道口子，血顺着裤腿流到台上。那师兄的金刃是一口气一口气发的，发一道，喘一口——跟当年的卢方一样。他等的是那一口喘。等到第十一道，那师兄一身的灵力全在刃上，胸前那层光薄了一霎，小满的火柴进去了——不是进人，是进那口喘：剑尖抵在那师兄胸口的衣襟上，停住了。那师兄低头看了看剑尖，看了很久，往后退了一步，退出了台边。掉下台的，输。执事的锣槌在手里转了两转：「沈小满，胜。」

这一回没有猪蜻蜓，也没有镜子，五场，一场一场打下来，打得规规矩矩，台下的人都说没意思。只有小满自己知道，决赛那一剑要是晚一霎，先退出台边的是他。肋下那道口子，缝了七针，长了半个月。周衡把那本蓝布面的名录翻到新的一页，提起笔来，写了「沈小满」三个字，笔停了一停——三百年的名录上，头一回写一个杂灵根的名字。观主把玉盒子放在他手里，封条上盖着大印。

钱掌柜在老槐树底下收摊。阿禾把那张纸条摊在秤盘上，一个字也没说。钱掌柜叹了一口气，解开布袋，一文一文往秤盘上数：「一，二，三……」数得极慢，数一文，嘴角往下耷拉一分。数到二十，围上来七八个人；数到四十，围了一圈，那张胖脸已皱成了一只苦瓜。数到五十，钱掌柜的手在袋口停了一停，又摸出一文，搁在最上头：「本钱。」

阿禾把五十一文拢进帕子里，摸出小本子，翻到五年前那一页。那一页上只一行：**一文。利息另算。**她在底下添了一笔。

钱掌柜把板子往肩上一扛，走出两步，又回过头来，冲小满背上那张弓一抬下巴：「那木头，打听出名字没有？」五年，他年年腊月扛板子上山，见了小满，头一句都是这一句。小满道：「没有。」钱掌柜道：「不急。」

当夜小满在柴房里揭了封条，盒盖一开，一股药气又苦又腥；一道纹，纹边两三点黑斑，一转，下品；饭桶闻了一口，盖上那只小兽拿鼻孔对着他，「噗」地喷出一小股黑烟，炉盖「啪」地一合，再不理他。他讨了半碗米汤，把封条粘了回去，连玉盒子收进储物袋里——全天下唯一一颗他拿出来说得清来历的[筑基丹]{注=foundation-pill}。

第二天他从正殿西北角过，闵丹师正从丹房里出来，两个人打了个照面。五年，隔着一口炉子，一个看火，一个看他。闵丹师的鼻子动了一动——守了三十年炉子的人，鼻子比眼睛灵——目光在他腰上那只储物袋上停了一停。他什么也没说，走了。

这五年，漳水边上，每年十月十八，推下去一只船，船上坐一个穿嫁衣的姑娘。五年，五只船。沉鼎观离漳水十天的路，观里没有一个人知道她们叫什么。周衡知道是哪一天。
story.en:
That winter he passed layer eight.

Every year on the eighteenth of the tenth month Zhou Heng did not open his ledger all day, and did not break his night-watch candle in half; every New Year's Eve he went once to the main hall and came out with the same sentence, "Next year I'll come again." Xiaoman did not ask. Qin Yan laid her Foundation in the fifth year and was sent to errands elsewhere; Sun Ergou climbed a layer every two years, one to three, and cried once at the door of the long bunk each time; A-He sowed her strip of earth every year, and every year most of the ears were empty. Old Qu gave him one rule, and one only: "Errands, you may go. The Mengshan tags, you don't touch — the man on the other side of that mirror knows where you come from." Letters came twice a year, his mother's hand still small and dense: the roof doesn't leak now; your father's knee hurts when it's overcast, and when it's clear too. Not one inner-court room of his own came free, and he still slept in the bunk nearest the door of that west-wing room. The contest came round every year; the first few years he didn't go up — he was not yet at layer nine, and had he won that Foundation pill he could only have carried it about, and drawn the whole temple's eyes.

What Old Qu taught that summer was called a form, but was really one sentence. Xiaoman asked him: "Master, the bear's roar — why was it bound to come?" "Because it can't hold," said Old Qu. He recited a line: "The *Daodejing* says: 'A gale does not last a morning; a cloudburst does not last a day.' A great wind can't blow a whole morning, a downpour can't fall a whole day. What heaven and earth can't keep up — can it?" He lit a candle and set it on the bluestone. "Try blowing it out." Xiaoman puffed out his cheeks and blew with all he had; the flame lay flat along the candle, flattened to a line, and would not go out; when he was out of breath it stood up again, just as before. "You can't blow it out," said Old Qu. "When you are out of breath, it's still there. Stilling the wind isn't standing still. It's waiting for the blowing to end."

Only then did he see it: the seven bites on the dyke, the three turns on the shore, the bear's roar — all one thing.

From eight to nine, Old Qu taught Advance-and-retreat. It was autumn; he tapped the broom handle on the ground: "In the *Book of Changes*, the first line of the hexagram Xun opens with two words: 'advance, retreat.' The whole line is: 'First six: advancing and retreating — it profits a warrior to hold firm.'" He wrote the six characters on the bluestone with the handle. "Advancing and retreating is a mind not made up; the one who is made up is the warrior — one stroke out, all the qi, no half kept back for retreating." He pointed at a pine bough at the cliff edge as thick as a bowl's mouth: "Cut it."

Xiaoman cut. The sword stuck in the bough and would not come out — he had put most of a breath into it and kept a little back, afraid of cutting air and not recovering. "You kept a breath back for yourself," said Old Qu. Xiaoman pulled the sword free and cut again, and this time pressed the whole of the qi in his dantian into the blade and kept nothing; the bough came down with a crack, the sword went through and he with it, could not stop, lurched two steps before he stood, not a drop of qi left in the jar, his legs like noodles. "That is advance-and-retreat," said Old Qu. He looked down the cliff and added, so low it could hardly be heard: "The sword of this palace, Xun the fourth, does not fear slow and does not fear soft; it fears advance-and-retreat. Half-way in and wanting to back out, and the stroke falls apart on its own." A pause. "…The sword is like that. Other things, too."

Xiaoman did not understand then what that last sentence had been added for. Before the twelfth month that year he was at layer nine; between the in-breath and the out, no seam could be heard. At nine the Matchstick threw a thin line of sparks off its point with every stroke, fine as what spits out of a stove — he did not know what it was, and Old Qu did not say.

That autumn, in the little room behind the pill house, he had a furnace of his own. It was one Pill-master Min had spoiled and thrown out, a crack down the wall daubed over with clay, three pills to a batch. Pill-master Min said only: "Grind your own, watch your own fire. If you burn it, grind it for binder." The first batch, all three burnt. The second, two burnt and one never turned — a lump of black. The fifth batch gave one pill, pale jade, one ring, lopsided, like a child's writing. He carried it to Pill-master Min, who picked it up, turned it, smelled it, and said: "It has fire in it." And: "It can be eaten." In five years that was the longest praise he heard from Pill-master Min's mouth. From then on, when anyone asked about the pills in his hand, he said: "I made them." That sentence was true; and the Rice Tub's one-ring and two-ring pills mixed in among the one-ring pills he made himself, and no one could tell them apart — except in one way: his had fire in them, and the Rice Tub's had none. He held one of the Rice Tub's up to his own furnace a long while and thought: what if I put it in, and passed it through the fire once? He did not. He put the pill back in his jacket.

That year in the twelfth month Shopkeeper Qian carried his board up the mountain as always and set out his stall under the old locust tree. The first few lines on the board were inner court, as ever; the very last line read: **Shen Xiaoman — one pays fifty.**

Someone asked: "Layer nine now, and still one pays fifty?" Shopkeeper Qian worked his abacus. "A five-door false root taking first — not once in three hundred years." Another flick. "Four years and he's not been up on the platform. The Shen Xiaoman the whole temple remembers is the one at layer four, covered in blood, hanging over a branch like washing — him at layer nine in a fight, who's seen that? What I haven't seen, I write long."

A-He squeezed up to the scale pan and put down one cash. Shopkeeper Qian lifted his eyelids. "Young lady, five years ago you bet on him once." "I lost," said A-He. "Betting again?" said Shopkeeper Qian. "Four years he hasn't gone up," said A-He. "I had nowhere to bet." She took her slip, tucked it away, and left. That year, the whole stake on Shen Xiaoman came to one cash.

At Laba in the fifth year the wind was from the north. In the first bout Xiaoman drew an inner-court fire-root at layer nine. He got up on the platform, and the first thing he looked at was not the man but the flag at the edge of the training ground — it streamed south. Wind first, then the deer; there was no one behind him to say it, so he said it himself. He stepped onto the northern slab and did not budge. The senior's fireballs came one after another; he took them on earth walls, one wall smashed for each ball, till the platform was all smoke; and the smoke went with the north wind, all of it south — into the senior's own eyes. The senior coughed once and gave half a step; coughing up a fistful of tears and snot, and by the seventh cough he had backed to the edge. Only then did Xiaoman walk over and give him one push. Off the platform, you lose.

Three bouts in the middle: one won with his feet, one by counting, one because the man across from him lost his head — not one of them good to watch. His opponent in the final was an inner-court layer nine at Consummation who had waited nine years for that pill, all out from the first step onto the stage, metal blade after metal blade. What Xiaoman could dodge he dodged; what he could not, he went with — Going-with-the-wind, the sword laid along the blade and turning it aside, half its force shed, the other half still ploughing him half a foot backwards, the thick soil under his feet holding; the few he could not turn, he took. By the time the half-stick of incense was half burnt his left side was open under the ribs, blood running down his trouser leg onto the boards. The man's blades came one breath at a time — a blade, then a gasp — the same as Lu Fang had, years ago. It was that gasp he waited for. At the eleventh blade all the man's qi was in the edge, the light over his chest thinned for an instant, and Xiaoman's Matchstick went in — not into the man, into that gasp: the point rested on the front of his robe over the heart, and stopped. The man looked down at the point, looked a long time, and took one step back — off the edge of the stage. Off the stage, and you have lost. The steward's mallet turned twice in his hand: "Shen Xiaoman wins."

This time there was no pig-copter and no mirror: five bouts, fought one after another, all by the book, and the crowd said it was dull. Only Xiaoman knew that had that last stroke come an instant later, it would have been he who stepped off the edge first. The cut under his ribs took seven stitches and half a month.

Shopkeeper Qian was packing up under the old locust tree. A-He spread her slip on the scale pan and said not a word. Shopkeeper Qian sighed, untied his bag, and began counting onto the scale pan one cash at a time: "One, two, three…" — very slowly, the corners of his mouth sagging a notch with every coin. By twenty, seven or eight people had gathered; by forty, there was a ring of them, and his fat face had shriveled into a bitter gourd. At fifty, Shopkeeper Qian's hand stopped at the mouth of the bag; then he took out one more cash and laid it on top. "Your stake."

A-He gathered the fifty-one cash into her handkerchief, took out her little notebook, and turned to the page from five years ago. On it was just the one line: **One cash. Interest charged separately.** Beneath it she added a note.

Shopkeeper Qian swung the board onto his shoulder, went two steps, turned back, and jerked his chin at the bow on Xiaoman's back: "That wood — found out its name yet?" Five years he had carried his board up the mountain every twelfth month, and every year, seeing Xiaoman, that was the first thing he said. "No," said Xiaoman. "No hurry," said Shopkeeper Qian.

That night in the woodshed Xiaoman lifted the seal; the lid opened on a smell both bitter and rank: one ring, two or three dark flecks beside it, one-turn, low grade; the Rice Tub sniffed it once, the little beast on its lid turned its nostrils on him and went "pfft!" — a puff of black smoke — the lid slammed shut, and would have nothing more to do with him. He begged half a bowl of rice water, glued the seal back down, and put it, jade box and all, into the storage pouch — the one Foundation pill in all the world whose history he could tell.

Next day, passing the north-west corner of the main hall, he met Pill-master Min coming out of the pill house. Five years, across one furnace: one watching the fire, one watching him. Pill-master Min's nose twitched — thirty years at a furnace and the nose is sharper than the eyes — and his gaze rested a moment on the storage pouch at Xiaoman's belt. He said nothing, and went on.

In those five years, every eighteenth of the tenth month, a boat was pushed out on the Zhang with a girl in a bridal gown sitting in it. Five years, five boats. Chending Temple was ten days from the Zhang, and no one in it knew their names. Zhou Heng knew which day it was.

exits.means: the autumn month: the lake brims over, layer nine, Consummation; his master calls him up the cliff

refuse.zh: 一季一季来：先过了前头那一季。
refuse.en: One season at a time: finish the one before first.

story.zh:
没过多少日子，丹田里那口水缸满得往外直漾，吸进去一口灵气，便溢出来一口，再也添不进去了——外门的人管这个叫「九层巅峰」；褚先生的名册上，只写四个字：九层圆满。

八月里，瞿老叫他上了一趟崖顶。
story.en:
Before many days had passed, the great jar in his dantian was brimming over: breathe in one breath of spirit and one spilled out; nothing more would go in — the outer court called this "the peak of layer nine"; in Master Chu's register it was written in four characters only: layer nine, Consummation.

In the eighth month, Old Qu called him up to the clifftop.
